1.title: the oldest hello
1.hook: you've said it after yoga class; the words inside say more than hello
1.carry: the light in me sees the light in you
1.howItsDone: Hindus greet one another with namaste or namaskar, palms pressed together at the chest and the head slightly bowed. The same gesture is made to elders, to guests and before images of the gods.

segments.voice: You've said it at the end of a yoga class, and you've probably heard it means the light in me sees the light in you. The word itself says something much simpler. The longer meaning is a reading of it, and that reading comes from somewhere specific. First, a guess.

Namaste is Sanskrit, and it splits in two. Namas: a bow. Te: to you. Word for word, I bow to you. That's the whole dictionary meaning. So where does the light come from? From a reading of the word. One of the oldest Hindu texts describes a light that shines above the heavens, above everything, and then says that same light is the light inside a person. Out there and in here: one light. Put that next to a bow and you get the popular line: the light in me sees the light in you. Not a translation. An interpretation, with a real source behind it. What the reading changes is who you're bowing to. Not someone's job, mood or résumé, but whatever in them is the same as what's in you. And nobody has to earn it first. In this reading, it's already there.

2.title: the sound the universe hums
2.hook: the sound a room makes together; it's three sounds and a silence
2.tomorrow: the thing that's yours to do
2.howItsDone: Hindus chant om at the start of prayers, mantras and readings of scripture, often at the end too, and it is written as a single sacred sign, ॐ, in homes and temples.

segments.voice: Yesterday: namaste. Namas, a bow; te, to you. Today, the sound that opens almost every Hindu prayer.

Om. A yoga class ends with it, and a lot of Hindu prayers begin with it. Most people treat it as one long hum. One of the oldest Hindu texts hears four parts in it: three sounds, and a fourth that isn't a sound at all. First, a guess.

Say it slowly and you can feel three sounds. A, with the mouth open. U, as the lips round. M, as they close. That's why it's sometimes written aum. An old text of just twelve verses starts by saying om is all of this: past, present, future, and whatever lies beyond time. Then it maps the sounds onto your day. A is waking, the world you can see and touch. U is dreaming, the world made of the mind. M is deep, dreamless sleep, where nothing is wanted. The fourth part has no sound. It's the silence after the m runs out, and the text calls it simply the fourth: the self, at peace. So om isn't a sign-off. It's a map of a whole day in one breath, with the quiet underneath it. The Bhagavad Gita says acts of offering, giving and discipline begin with it.
screen: `A — WAKING.` · `U — DREAMING.` · `M — DEEP SLEEP.` · `THE FOURTH — THE SILENCE.`

segments.voice: One breath with the bell. Breathe in. Let it out as the sound, aloud or under your breath: a, u, m. Let the m run out on its own, then stay a second in the quiet after it. That quiet is the fourth part.
Om. A, u and m for waking, dreaming and deep sleep, and the silence after it for the fourth. Second word on your strand.

3.title: the thing that's yours to do
3.hook: a warrior puts down his bow and says he no longer knows what's right
3.carry: do the thing that's yours to do
3.howItsDone: Hindus speak of dharma as right action and the order that holds life together, and also of svadharma, one's own duty in a given place and stage of life; the Bhagavad Gita is read and recited as a guide to it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: om, three sounds and a silence. Today, the word at the center of the Bhagavad Gita.

The Bhagavad Gita opens on a battlefield. A warrior named Arjuna asks his charioteer to drive him out between the two armies, and he sees his own family on the other side: teachers, uncles, cousins. His bow slips from his hand and he sits down in the chariot. The word he reaches for, to say what he's lost, is today's word.

Dharma gets translated as duty, law or religion, and each of those catches only a piece. It comes from a Sanskrit root meaning to hold, or to support. Dharma is what holds things up: teachers say the dharma of fire is to burn and the dharma of water is to flow. It's what a thing is for, the part it holds in the whole. In the Gita's second chapter, Arjuna says his mind is confused about dharma, and he asks his charioteer, Krishna, to teach him. The rest of the Gita is that teaching. One line from the third chapter shows where it starts: better your own dharma, even done imperfectly, than someone else's done well. Your own dharma is svadharma. So dharma isn't only rules handed down. It's also a question: what is mine to do here? Arjuna isn't missing information. He's lost the thread of what's his to do.

Your line: do the thing that's yours to do. It's the question the whole Gita answers, and this path comes back to it. Day three.

4.title: why it's said three times
4.hook: om shanti shanti shanti: three times, never once, and there's a reason
4.tomorrow: why Indian kids touch their grandparents' feet
4.howItsDone: Hindu prayers, readings and ceremonies often close with om shanti shanti shanti, the word for peace said three times.

segments.voice: Yesterday: dharma, what holds things up. Today, a word you've probably heard said three times in a row.

Om shanti shanti shanti. It closes a lot of Hindu prayers, and more than a few yoga classes. Not once, not twice: three times. That isn't just for the rhythm. Traditional teachers read the three as a list. First, a guess at the word.

Shanti means peace, the settled kind: calm water with nothing stirring it. The Bhagavad Gita puts it bluntly: for someone without peace, how can there be happiness? Now the three. Traditional teachers read the three shantis as three kinds of trouble, the three places a bad day can come from. Trouble from forces beyond anyone's control: storms, floods, the world. Trouble from other beings: the friend who didn't call, the driver who cut in. And trouble from within: your own body and your own mind. Three sources, three shantis. The teachers add something practical. There's little anyone can do about the first, more about the second, and the third is the one most within reach, and the easiest to skip. So the chant isn't padding. It goes down the list: peace out there, peace between us, peace in here.
screen: `SHANTI — THE SETTLED KIND.` · `THE WORLD.` · `OTHER PEOPLE.` · `YOUR OWN MIND.`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell, one shanti on each, said silently. First out-breath: toward the world. Second: toward one person you're not at peace with. You don't have to forgive them. Third: toward your own mind.
Shanti. Peace, the settled kind, said three times: the world, other people, your own mind. Fourth word.
Your line: peace, peace, peace. Next time something rattles you, there are three places it could have come from. That's day four.

5.title: why Indian kids touch their grandparents' feet
5.hook: a child bends to an elder's feet, and a hand comes down on the child's head
5.carry: bow to what came before you
5.howItsDone: In Hindu families, children and younger adults greet parents, grandparents and teachers with pranam, often bending to touch their feet, and the elder answers with a hand on the head and a blessing.

segments.voice: Yesterday: shanti, three times over. Today, a gesture you may have seen at a family gathering.

A grandmother walks in, and before anyone says hello, a twelve-year-old bends down and touches her feet. Her hand rests on the child's head for a second. Then everyone goes back to arguing about dinner. From the outside it can look like bowing to a boss. Inside the gesture, something goes both ways.

Pranam is Sanskrit: pra, forward, and nam, to bend. To bend forward, a respectful greeting. It shares its root with namaste. Touching the feet has its own name, charan sparsh: charan, the feet; sparsh, a touch. One common explanation: the head is the high point of a person, where the pride sits, and the feet have walked further down the road than yours. The high point of you meets the low point of them. Then the other half. The elder's hand comes down on the head: an ashirvad, a blessing given back. Respect goes one way, a blessing comes the other, and nobody walks away smaller. In a lot of families, children learn to do it at weddings and visits long before anyone explains why. The why is simple: nobody invents themselves. Somebody walked the road first, and the gesture says you noticed.

segments.voice: One breath with the bell. Bring to mind one person who made your road easier: a grandparent, a teacher, anyone, living or not. As you breathe out, bow your head to them a little, for real. Stay down for one more breath.
Pranam. To bend forward: a bow to the ones who walked first, and a blessing that comes back. Fifth word.
Your line: bow to what came before you. Somebody walked the road first. That's day five.

6.title: the one at every doorway
6.hook: an elephant-headed figure on the dashboard, by the door, at the top of the page
6.howItsDone: Hindus honor Ganesha first at ceremonies, weddings and new beginnings, keep his image near doorways and in shops, and some write shri ganeshaya namah at the top of a page before starting to write.

segments.voice: Yesterday: pranam, the bow and the blessing that comes back. Today you meet someone.

A small statue on a taxi dashboard. A picture above a shop counter. His name printed at the top of a wedding invitation, before anyone else's. Elephant head, round belly, one tusk broken. He sits wherever things start, and that's the clue to who he is.

Start with the name. Ganesha is gana plus isha: lord of the ganas, the attendants of the god Shiva. But the title that explains the doorways is Vighnaharta. Vighna, an obstacle; harta, one who removes. The remover of obstacles. That's why he's honored first: before a ceremony, a wedding, a new shop or an exam. Some people write shri ganeshaya namah at the top of a page before they begin, and namah is the same bow as in namaste. There's a popular way of reading his body: big ears, listen more than you talk; small eyes, focus; a big belly, take in what life serves, good and hard. And the broken tusk: tradition says he wrote down the Mahabharata as the sage Vyasa dictated it, and one story says that when his pen gave out, he snapped off his own tusk and kept writing.

7.title: a handrail made of sound
7.hook: your mind already loops a phrase all day; a mantra is choosing which one
7.tomorrow: what your grandmother was actually doing
7.howItsDone: Hindus repeat mantras aloud, in a whisper or silently, sometimes counting them on a string of prayer beads called a mala; this repetition is called japa, and the Gayatri mantra is recited at dawn and dusk by some families.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ganesha, the remover of obstacles. Six words so far: namaste, om, dharma, shanti, pranam, Ganesha. Today, the seventh.

A song from the grocery store gets stuck in your head and loops until lunch. Or it's last night's argument, replaying on its own. Nobody chose it. Minds repeat things. The practice of mantra starts from that fact and asks a practical question: if the mind is going to repeat something anyway, what if you chose it?

Mantra comes from man, to think, and tra, an instrument. An instrument of thought: a tool for the mind. A traditional explanation hears a second meaning in tra, protection: a mantra protects the mind that holds it. You've already met three this week: om, om shanti shanti shanti, and shri ganeshaya namah. One of the best known is the Gayatri mantra, a very old verse that many Hindus say every morning. It asks the light of the sun to wake up and guide our thoughts. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says that among offerings he is japa, the quiet repetition of a mantra. How does it work? The mind can only hold so much at once. When it's holding the mantra, there's less room for the loop. Less like a spell, more like a handrail on a dark staircase: when the loop comes back, you go back to the rail.
screen: `MAN — TO THINK. TRA — A TOOL.` · `OM, SHANTI, THE GAYATRI.` · `AMONG OFFERINGS, I AM JAPA.` · `THE LOOP COMES BACK. SO DO YOU.`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell. On each out-breath, say om silently. If something else drifts in, a song or a worry, don't push it away. Just go back to om. The coming back is the practice.
Mantra. An instrument of thought, repeated on purpose. Seventh word: a week's worth.

man, to think, and tra, an instrument: a tool for the mind.

original.note: Sanskrit: man, to think, plus tra, an instrument. an instrument of thought.

trapdoor: what you thought: a chant, or a catchy motto.
what it means: a tool for the mind, repeated on purpose, so the mind has something to hold.
what a scholar hears: man + tra, an instrument of thought; a traditional gloss hears trana, protection. Gita 10.25: among offerings, japa.

story.title: the robber who couldn't say the name
story.text: A well-loved telling says the poet Valmiki started out as a robber. One day he tried to rob the sage Narada, who asked him a question: would his family share the weight of what he did? They said no. Shaken, he asked to change, and Narada gave him the name Rama to repeat. He couldn't bring himself to say it, so he said mara, mara, over and over, until it ran together into Rama, Rama. He sat repeating it so long that an anthill grew over him. Valmika means anthill. He came out as Valmiki, who would compose the Ramayana.
story.source: a traditional telling of Valmiki's life (later than the Ramayana itself)

wrong.myth: a mantra is a magic spell.
wrong.truth: the word itself says what it is: man, to think, and tra, a tool. less like a spell, more like a handrail.
